etymologies.etymologyHTML: Formed under the influence of both diminue (from Old French diminuer, from Latin dīminuo) and minish.

quote.citation: 2012 December 14, Simon Jenkins, “We mustn't overreact to North Korea boys' toys”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 188, number 2, page 23:
quote.text: The threat of terrorism to the British lies in the overreaction to it of British governments. Each one in turn clicks up the ratchet of surveillance, intrusion and security. Each one diminishes liberty.

quote.citation: 2013 July 20, “Old soldiers?”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8845:
quote.text: Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine. […] One thing that is true, though, is that murder rates have fallen over the centuries, as policing has spread and the routine carrying of weapons has diminished. Modern society may not have done anything about war. But peace is a lot more peaceful.

quote.citation: 2021 December 15, Robin Leleux, “Awards honour the best restoration  projects: The Bam Nuttall Partnership Award: Kilmarnock”, in RAIL, number 946, page 58:
quote.text: In the latter years of its existence, BR was rationalising its estate by pulling down station buildings which were too large for its modern operational needs, or by shutting off parts of them when demolition was not an option. Kilmarnock station falls into this latter category. It dominates the townscape, but its operational importance has seriously diminished since electrification of the West Coast Main Line.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To lessen the authority or dignity of; to put down; to degrade; to abase; to weaken; to nerf (in gaming).

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Ezekiel 29:15:
quote.text: It shall be the basest of the kingdoms; neither shall it exalt itself any more above the nations: for I will diminish them, that they shall no more rule over the nations.

quote.citation: 1639, Ralph Robinson (translator), Utopia by Thomas More, London, Book 2, “Of their journying or travelling abroad,” p. 197,[1]
quote.text: […]  this doth nothing diminish their opinion.

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, Paradise Lost‎[2], Book 4, lines 32-35:
quote.text: O thou, that, with surpassing glory crowned,Lookest from thy sole dominion like the GodOf this new world; at whose sight all the starsHide their diminished heads; to thee I call,

quote.citation: 1961, V. S. Naipaul, chapter 3, in A House for Mr Biswas, London: André Deutsch:
quote.text: In Seth’s presence Mr Biswas felt diminished. Everything about Seth was overpowering: his calm manner, his smooth grey hair, his ivory holder, his hard swollen forearms  […]

quote.citation: 1853, Elizabeth Gaskell, chapter 8, in Cranford‎[3], London: J.M. Dent, published 1904, page 120:
quote.text: The chair and table legs diminished as they neared the ground, and were straight and square in all their corners.

quote.citation: 1948, Graham Greene, The Heart of the Matter‎[4], Penguin, published 1971, Part Two, Chapter 2, 1, p. 77:
quote.text: ‘Good evening, good evening,’ Father Rank called. His stride lengthened and he caught a foot in his soutane and stumbled as he went by. ‘A storm’s coming up,’ he said. ‘Got to hurry,’ and his ‘ho, ho, ho’ diminished mournfully along the railway track, bringing no comfort to anyone.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 4:2:
quote.text: Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it, that ye may keep the commandments of the Lord your God which I command you.
